flags.why: Text matches print: "both Grey and Green Linnets". "Grey Linnets" is not a substring here; wording of an elliptical name ("Grey" vs "Grey and Green Linnets") is a judgement call.
Same sentence: "enormous numbers crossed in the autumn, commencing Aug. 7th ...; from thence to Sept. 18th, almost daily". The crossing covers this clause, so seen is too weak.
"late in afternoon. Meadow Pipits, great flights. Tree Pipits less": the time must lead what follows, but the full stops leave open how far it reaches.
"scattered flocks of Wild Ducks, about seven in number": whether "about seven" counts flocks or ducks is unclear. Taking "scattered flocks" as the count is allowed.
"Sept. 27th, 10\na.m., a large flock of small birds containing many Robins": the time is stated for these birds.
"one passing\nS.E.": the rules give direction as the verb plus the point ("passing S."), so "passing S.E." is right.
"one struck and caught": struck is stated. Caught should be a separate record (one per behaviour), so this record isn't wrong.
The record copies the text's "7.80 p.m." exactly; the print reads 7.30, so the slip is in the transcription.
"two _Crossbills_ flew on board. Both were captured": "Both" is the printed count for the capture clause.
The text reads "_Tardus Naumanii_" and the record copies it; the print reads Turdus, so the transcription has the slip.
"Oct. 4th, 1 to 2 a.m., ... and three birds killed": one sentence, so the time covers the birds killed.
"a great number of Larks, 8 p.m., ... haze. Great numbers struck": a new sentence, so it's unclear whether the time of the sighting covers the striking.
"three and a Starling caught": the Starling is a separately named bird and gets its own record. The Chaffinches ("three") belong in another record.
For the Starling record the count is "a" ("a Starling caught"). "three" belongs to the Chaffinches.
"till midnight, some struck and fell overboard; three and a Starling caught": the clause continues after the semicolon, so it shares the time.
